summary: A reply defending the Telnet Go-Ahead mechanism against objections in RFC 596. The author argues that disliking line-at-a-time systems is a matter of taste and that Go-Ahead will work well between reasonably implemented hosts.

plainLanguage.summary: One person said a certain signal for taking turns was bad. This note answers that it works fine and the complaint is mostly about style.

subtitle: A defense of the Telnet Go-Ahead signal as practical for line-at-a-time systems.

tldr.problem: A previous RFC (NIC 20812) argued that Telnet's Go-Ahead signal was unworkable and aesthetically wrong for line-at-a-time systems like those on IBM and other mainframes.
tldr.mechanism: The author argues that Go-Ahead actually works well when properly understood: it signals when the server is done sending output, allowing line-buffering systems to know when to expect user input and reducing overhead.
tldr.outcome: The Go-Ahead mechanism was retained in Telnet, becoming a standard way for hosts to signal turn-taking in terminal sessions, especially between systems with different input models.

today: RFC 595 is a historical record of a debate about Telnet design. Go-Ahead remains part of the Telnet specification (RFC 854). While Telnet itself has largely been replaced by SSH for security reasons, Go-Ahead principles inform how modern terminal protocols handle turn-taking.

sections.title: The Go-Ahead Debate
sections.content:
Go-Ahead is a signal in Telnet where the server tells the client that it has finished sending output and the user may now type. A previous RFC (NIC 20812) by Edward Taft argued that this mechanism was impractical and aesthetically wrong, particularly for line-at-a-time systems—computers that buffer user input until a full line is entered, then process it all at once.

RFC 595, written by Wayne Hathaway of AMES-67, defends Go-Ahead as practical and even essential for such systems.
sections.plainLanguage: One expert said 'Your turn to talk' signals do not work. This note shows they actually work great for computers that wait for whole lines of typing.

sections.title: Line-at-a-Time Systems and the Benefit
sections.content:
Line-at-a-time systems (LAAT) buffer characters at a controller or front-end until the user presses Enter. The application does not see partial lines. This design saves CPU interrupts but creates a problem in Telnet: how does a line-buffering client know when the server has finished sending output so it is safe to accept user input?

Go-Ahead solves this by signaling 'I am done sending, it is your turn now.' For LAAT systems, this is as practical as turn-taking in a conversation: a pause (or Go-Ahead) shows it is time to respond. Hathaway argues that disliking LAAT systems is a matter of taste, not a reason to reject Go-Ahead.
sections.plainLanguage: Line-buffering computers need a signal saying 'Stop, wait for me to type a whole line.' Go-Ahead does that, just like a pause in conversation.

sections.title: Practical Implementation Concerns
sections.content:
Hathaway addresses specific objections: Go-Ahead should be sent when a system has reasonable assurance it is done sending (like after a prompt). If unexpected output arrives afterward, it is simply sent with another Go-Ahead; no harm done. For multi-line output (like editor printout), a single Go-Ahead at the end suffices.

The author also argues for allowing user TELNET programs to send Go-Ahead manually when needed, and notes that some problematic behaviors (like TENEX SNDMSG failing with Go-Ahead) were implementation bugs that should be fixed, not reasons to remove the feature.
sections.plainLanguage: Send Go-Ahead when you are probably done talking. If you say more, just send another one. It is that simple, and systems should be fixed to handle it.
